raw_signal_observation: The README states that every phone-browser connection is encrypted with TLS plus XChaCha20-Poly1305 and that data never leaves the local network. AndroidManifest.xml sets android:usesCleartextTraffic='true'. That manifest flag permits cleartext transport but does not prove that any product connection actually uses it.
material_claim: The cleartext permission is not sufficient evidence to refute the product's encryption promise. The actual HTTP server/client transport path or an integrated network fixture must be inspected before calling this a security defect or changing the manifest.
neta_next_move: Trace the local server and browser connection scheme/cipher path, then deliberately attempt a cleartext connection in an isolated fixture. If the product rejects/redirects it and all intended channels remain encrypted, the manifest permission is not enough to justify a product change.
reversal_condition: If the integrated path accepts a user-relevant plaintext connection covered by the README's 'every connection' wording, permit the narrow transport/manifest repair; otherwise retain the implementation and calibrate only claims that exceed the tested boundary.
baseline_decision: BUILD: set usesCleartextTraffic=false so the Android platform enforces the README's all-connections-encrypted promise instead of merely relying on application discipline.

evidence: Post-freeze source tracing found the Android Ktor/Netty server explicitly binding both an HTTP connector and an HTTPS sslConnector on configured ports; the HTTP connector binds on all interfaces.

Post-freeze issue #320 (2026) reports a real user opening Web Access successfully at an http://...:8080 address in a browser, independently confirming that a user-relevant HTTP path exists rather than the manifest merely permitting unused cleartext.

The repository also contains XChaCha20-Poly1305 application-layer crypto, so the revealed evidence specifically contradicts the literal TLS-on-every-connection wording; it does not establish that HTTP payloads are unencrypted at the application layer.
adjudication.decision_delta: SURVIVED: Neta refused to infer a live cleartext path from the manifest alone. The discriminator then found a real HTTP connector and external 2026 use of it, materially sharpening the problem from 'manifest permission looks unsafe' to an explicit product-contract decision about supporting HTTP versus claiming TLS on every connection. The baseline's immediate manifest flip could break an actually used path and was therefore premature.
adjudication.lesson: HOLDOUT score only until Wave 1 closes. Permission to use a transport is not proof that the transport is used; once use is confirmed, keep transport-layer and application-layer encryption claims separate and repair the actual contract boundary rather than the proxy.
